name: Leaning Tower of Pisa

facts.label: from the first stone to the bells

modelNote: Dimensions, storeys, columns and dates from the sources. The lean before 1990 is schematic: only 5.5° (1990) and 3.97° (2001) are documented. The slight curve of the upper floors is not modelled.

evidence.identity: Torre di Pisa, Piazza del Duomo, Pisa, Italy (OSM relation 12982355)
features: A hollow cylinder of white marble, 15.484 m across at the base, walls 2.44 m thick (Wikipedia).
Eight storeys: a ground floor of blind arcades on engaged columns, six open galleries of 30 columns each, and a smaller bell chamber with seven bells (italia.it, Wikipedia).
A lean to the south: 5.5° in 1990, 3.97° since 2001 (Wikipedia, Burland et al.).
evidence.geometry: Outer radius 7.742 m (Wikipedia); the OSM outline (radius 8.25 m) includes the footing. Total height 56 m shared between storeys from the photo taken from the east: ground floor about 1.8 gallery heights, bell chamber about 1.3, its radius about 0.65 of the tower's.
uncertainties: Storey heights and bell chamber size read from photos.
15 blind arches on the ground floor and 12 openings in the bell chamber counted on photos.
Lean before 1990 schematic; the gradual change of the masons' corrections (the curve of the upper floors) is not modelled.
Split of the upper galleries between 1272–1278 and 1319 inferred from the dates in the sources.

phases.title: The first three levels
phases.text: Foundations are laid on 9 August 1173. When the masons reach the second floor in 1178, the soft ground gives way and the tower begins to sink. Work stops.

moments.title: A hollow cylinder
moments.text: 15.48 m across at the base, with walls 2.44 m thick: a ring of white marble around a shaft 7.37 m wide.

phases.title: A century of waiting
phases.text: Pisa is at war, and the work stops for most of a century. The pause gives the ground time to settle under the weight of the first floors.

moments.title: The pause that saved it
moments.text: Without these hundred years for the soil to settle, the tower would almost certainly have toppled.

phases.title: Floors taller on one side
phases.text: Work resumes in 1272 under Giovanni di Simone. To make up for the tilt, the upper floors are built with one side taller than the other.

moments.title: Correcting a lean in stone
moments.text: Each new floor is taller on the leaning side, so the tower rises with a slight curve instead of a straight line.

phases.title: The seventh floor
phases.text: After another halt in 1278, the seventh floor is completed in 1319: six galleries of thirty columns now stand on the ground floor.

moments.title: 180 columns
moments.text: Six rings of galleries with thirty columns each stand on the blind arcades of the ground floor.

phases.title: The bell chamber
phases.text: Tommaso di Andrea Pisano adds the bell chamber, a smaller ring at the top. The tower is finished 199 years after its first stone.

moments.title: Seven bells
moments.text: The bell chamber holds seven bells, one for each note of the major scale.

phases.title: Closed at 5.5°
phases.text: On 7 January 1990 the tower is closed to the public: its tilt has reached 5.5 degrees. The bells are taken down and cables are tied around the third level.

moments.title: 870 tonnes of lead
moments.text: From 1993, 870 tonnes of lead counterweights on the raised side straighten the tower slightly.

phases.title: Straightened by 45 cm
phases.text: 38 m³ of soil are drawn out from under the raised side. The tilt falls to 3.97°, back to where it was in 1838, and the tower reopens on 15 December 2001.

moments.title: Still for the first time
moments.text: In May 2008, engineers announce that the tower has stopped moving for the first time in its history.
